After a component is 3D printed for the AMEC process, it needs to be coated with a ceramic slurry before it can be buried in sand for the casting process. This coating helps create a smooth outer surface for the casting, prevent sand erosion, and allow gas to escape during vaporization. Skuld conducted some testing of these coatings with a focus on improving the drying time for the coating. The results showed that alcohol-based coatings could reduce the drying time by up to 90%. 1.2.2 Basic Computational Model Development of the computational model began with an input of material property data for the 3D printing filament, PLA. This included thermodynamic parameters for pyrolysis and material kinetics. This data reaffirms the use of PLA because of the limited char yield as well as limited condensable and non- condensable gases (40% and 58% respectively). These qualities of PLA can be attributed to its low melting point and corn-based precursor material rather than hydrocarbons as seen in other polymers. The material parameters for PLA were then combined with the material properties for sand, aluminum 356, and IN17-4PH (a martensitic, precipitation hardening stainless steel). This includes parameters such as density, permeability, thermal conductivity, and specific heat. With these parameters, modeling could begin with the interaction at the surface between the molten metal and the polymer shell. With a fundamental understanding of the material properties and their behavior, a basic model was built using this information as an input. The goal of this model is to understand how the molten metal flows and interacts with the polymer shell. To test the model, a mesh representation of a plate with riser and sprue was designed (Figure 2). Multiple simulations were then conducted to understand how this would behave in a sand mold with varying fraction solid values (Figure 3). Figure 2: Mesh representation of a plate with sprue and riser for simulating the casting process. (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) (f) Figure 3: Simulation results for the plate from Figure 2. Solid fraction varies for each simulation: 14.9, 21.1, 34.4, 40.7, 44.3, and 52.2%. At this time, the model is still in its infancy. It has the ability to simulate specific geometries, such as that of Figure 2. With additional development, the model and simulation will provide an understanding of how a specific part will behave with a specific polymer while casting a specific metal. During the process, it is known that the polymer will pyrolyze, but how quickly does that happen, how much heat can the polymer absorb, how much gas is created and where, and what stress concentrations are formed and where.
